title: What a Heat-Pump Rebate Adds
problem: Avangrid pays heat-pump rebates without knowing how much winter peak load each one adds, because meter data cannot yet tell whole-home electric heat from supplemental heat. The winter thermostat program now under discussion may shed almost nothing in the coldest hours, which are the hours the grid is built for.
specific_user: Scott, Program Director of Load Research and one of the judges. He decides how many winter kW each heat-pump rebate adds to the load forecast and which winter flexibility resource his team backs: the proposed winter thermostat program, EV managed charging, or batteries paired with rebates. The Customer Programs and Products Manager and the Director of Advanced Load Forecasting act on the same numbers.
solution: The inputs are the existing 25,653-home by 8,760-hour matrix, hourly temperature, the heat-pump rebate sample and the current class labels. First, the tool picks the top 20, 50 and 100 system hours in each season and checks them against the system peak dates Scott gave: 2 July for summer and 7 February for winter. Second, it fits each home's kW-versus-temperature curve below 60F and sorts electric-heat homes by curve shape: straight-line whole-home resistance, a curve that bends upward in deep cold (a heat pump with strip backup), or a small, flat response (supplemental or occupancy-driven heat). It checks these labels against the rebate homes. Third, it measures what a rebated heat pump really adds in the winter top hours, using rebate homes against matched non-electric homes with the same cooling signature, split by curve shape. That number replaces the single-hour 3.29 kW and gives a flip count with a range. Fourth, it scores three winter flexibility options on the same top hours: a thermostat setback (sheds little in homes whose curve flattens at the coldest hours, because the heat is already running flat out), shifting the EV Level 2 load that falls in those hours, and winter battery relief from the peaky homes already ranked. The output is one table of kW added per rebate type, conversions to a winter peak, and the cheapest flexibility that covers it, plus a per-home heat-type column in customer_classes.csv.

The outputs are customer_actions.csv (one action per home), a chart of how many top hours each offer stack covers in MW, an Excel twin where the price assumptions and N can be edited, and a facts.json entry for every new number.

title: Top-Hours Firm Relief Screen
problem: Avangrid builds the grid to carry its top system hours, yet our battery list counts relief averaged over 4-hour windows on 10 event days. It also favours homes that stay heavily loaded for hours, the flat shape a 20 kWh battery cannot cover. So the MW we would hand a planner are not firm across the hours that set the build.
specific_user: The distribution planner in Reliability & Tech Processes who decides how many MW of residential flexibility (batteries, managed EV charging, thermostats) count as firm against the top 20 to 50 system hours before deferring or ordering capacity work. The second user is the storage program team that picks which homes to enroll.
solution: Inputs are the existing load matrix, system load series, weather, customer_classes.csv and the program battery (20.16 kWh, 7.68 kW, 89.4% round trip). Step 1 takes the sample's top N system hours (N = 20, 30, 50, as Scott suggested) for the year and per season, and checks them against Scott's system peak dates, 2 July and 7 February. Step 2 simulates battery dispatch against each home's load across every top-hour block, with an overnight recharge between back-to-back peak days. It reports firm relief (the kW cut in the home's worst top hour) and coverage (the share of the home's top-hour load above its baseline that the battery removes), so peaky homes score high and flat, high-load homes score low. Step 3 gives each home one lever and never counts a kW twice: managed charging for detected Level 2 homes, including the 392 that are not on the EV list; summer thermostat for AC homes; a battery only where coverage passes a threshold set from the curve; and a watch flag for flat winter electric-heat homes, because no winter lever is reliable yet. Output is top_hours_relief.csv (lever, firm kW and coverage for every home), a stacked chart of MW removed in each of the top 50 hours by lever beside today's 14.86 MW claim, and about 10 example shapes that explain the threshold.

title: Primary Heat Physics Test
solution: The tool reads the hourly AMI data and weather series the pipeline already loads for 25,653 homes and fits a few simple temperature regressions per home, vectorized so the method can scale to millions of meters. The first test checks whether the cold-weather load is there at night. A thermostat-run primary system has to cover the building's heat loss every hour, so it shows a kW-per-degree slope from 1 to 5 am. Space heaters follow people, so they show an evening slope with almost nothing overnight. The second test checks whether the load keeps climbing in the cold. A primary system keeps rising linearly down to the design temperature, while plug-in heaters level off at a fixed wattage. Curvature in the coldest temperature bin gives a heat pump versus resistance score with its confidence stated openly, since efficiency falls as it gets colder. The output is one auditable line per home with the overnight slope, the evening slope, the saturation flag, a class (primary, supplemental, uncertain or none) and its MW contribution across the top 20, 50 and 100 winter system hours, which is the measure Scott said flexibility is judged on. A roll-up then redoes the added kW per conversion using primary homes only and averaging over the top winter hours rather than one hour, and it reports the winter flip point as a range. Because Scott expects winter thermostat setbacks to struggle, the primary-heat homes go to conversion and battery offers rather than winter DR.

title: Primary Heat Finder for Coldest Hours
problem: Avangrid can see that a home's load climbs in the cold. It cannot tell whether that home heats mainly with electricity or only runs space heaters or a supplemental mini-split, and it cannot tell resistance heat from a heat pump. Without that split, the winter-peak forecast and the heat-pump program can't tell which homes actually drive the top winter hours, or whether a given conversion adds to them or cuts them.
specific_user: Scott, Program Director of Load Research, who keeps the electric-heat inventory. He called this split his team's hardest problem. He decides which homes count as electric-heat load in the inputs he gives Advanced Load Forecasting, and which homes he points customer programs to for heat-pump retrofits and winter flexibility.
solution: The tool reads the existing hourly matrix for 25,653 homes, the hourly weather, the current per-home classes and the heat-pump rebate list. Every temperature-responsive home gets three measurements. Persistence: does heat load hold through overnight cold hours and across consecutive cold days (primary heat), or does it show up only in occupied evening hours and level off (supplemental)? Slope shape below the balance point: a straight line looks like resistance; steepening in the coldest hours looks like a heat pump losing efficiency and switching on backup strips. Cooling signature: is there one? Threshold rules turn these into four tiers per home (primary resistance-like, primary heat-pump-like, supplemental, none), with a confidence level and a sensitivity range, and they are checked against the rebate list. For each tier the tool reports MW in the top 20, 30 and 50 winter system hours, plus a cold-snap peakiness score that says whether a battery could cover that home or whether its load is flat for too many hours. The winter flip point is then recomputed from primary-heat homes only, over the top hours instead of a single hour.

solution: Inputs are the existing 25,653 x 8,760 hourly matrix, the weather series, the electric-heat class from classify.py (2,873 to 4,143 homes), and the heat-pump rebate sample. heat_triage.py first sets the objective Scott named: the top 50 winter hours and top 50 summer hours of the sample, checked against his system peak dates (2 July 2026 and 7 February). It then sorts every electric-heat home into a tier using cold-day shape features. Primary electric heat keeps rising through the coldest hours and stays high across the day. A supplemental or space-heater home levels off and lifts only in the evening. A home that looks like dual fuel drops off below a balance point, which would explain why 48.3% of rebate homes show little heat. For each home the tool computes kW in the winter top hours, a peakiness score (whether a 7.68 kW / 20.16 kWh battery can cover the event, reusing bess.py), and winter kWh as bill exposure measured in kWh, so no tariff assumption is needed. The output is heat_triage.csv with a route per home and three slides. Peaky supplemental homes go to battery or winter DR. Primary-heat homes are excluded from winter setback events and offered resistance-to-heat-pump conversion and weatherization. Dual-fuel homes get backup-fuel switching on event days. Every route carries the MW it reaches at the top winter hours.

title: Top-Hours Flex Router
problem: Avangrid's grid is built for a few dozen top system hours, but it cannot tell, home by home, which flexibility resource would actually cut that home's load in those hours. So the scarce, expensive battery slots risk going to flat, high-load homes the battery cannot cover, while EV charging, which is cheap to shift, goes untargeted because half the EV list shows no home charging.
specific_user: The Customer Programs and Products Manager (a judge's role) decides which offer each home gets: managed EV charging, the summer thermostat event program, or one of the limited program batteries, and how many to fund. Load Research (Scott) uses the same output to show how many MW come off the top 20, 50 or 100 system hours in each season.
solution: Inputs are each home's 8,760 hourly AMI readings, weather, and the Part 1 flags we trust most: L2 charging, AC, seasonal and solar. The pipeline sums all 25,653 homes, finds the top N system hours per season (N = 20, 50, 100, following Scott), and replays those hours for every home under each resource. Managed charging moves detected L2 blocks out of those hours. The thermostat sheds the assumed 33% of AC weather load, summer only. The battery is dispatched at 20.16 kWh and 7.68 kW and recharges only outside the top hours, with the 3 kVA rule as a guardrail. The output is a per-home router file with a cheapest rung, a kW cut in each top hour and a coverage score, meaning the share of the home's top-hour excess the battery covers. That score is a "peakiness" threshold that sorts the whole customer base, rather than a hand-picked top-10 list. A stacked chart shows the MW removed at each of the top N system hours by resource. As a business, it is a per-meter screening service a utility reruns each season as EV and heat-pump adoption changes.

title: Electric Heat Census With Ranges
problem: Load research can see which homes use more power when it gets cold, but it cannot tell whether a home heats mainly with electricity, only uses space heaters to top up, or just spends more time indoors. Electric heat already carries about a third of winter peak-hour load, so the forecast's number of homes that heat mainly with electricity, and the split between resistance heat and heat pumps, can be wrong by more than a thousand homes, and nobody knows by how much.
specific_user: Scott, Avangrid's Program Director of Load Research. He signs off on how many homes heat with electricity and how many kW each group adds at peak, and those numbers go to Advanced Load Forecasting. He also decides which homes load research spends its verification and metering budget on. He named this split as the problem his team has struggled with most.
solution: Inputs: hourly AMI for the 25,653 homes, hourly weather, the pipeline's existing electric-heat and heat-pump scores, the heat-pump rebate list, and the seasonal-home flag. Method: every home that responds to temperature gets features that separate primary heat from top-up heat. The features are how steeply load climbs as it gets colder, whether that climb continues down to the coldest hours or flattens out the way plug-in heaters do, how much of the home's load falls in the system's top 20 and top 50 winter hours, and whether that load stays up overnight. Each home is then labelled primary electric heat, supplemental heat, or a temperature response without real heat. Primary-heat homes also get a resistance-or-heat-pump probability. The rebate list is treated as a biased sample of rebate recipients, not a random sample of owners. Output: an inventory per class with bootstrap 90% intervals across homes and thresholds, each class's kW in the system's top 20 and top 50 hours with a range, the 5,100-conversion winter-peaking crossover restated as a range, and a ranked list of homes to check against gas-service records first.

title: Cheapest-First Top-Hours Ladder
solution: Inputs are the existing 25,653 x 8,760 load matrix, the pipeline's appliance classes, and the program battery spec (7.68 kW, 20.16 kWh). The tool sums all homes to find the system's top 20, 50 and 100 hours in each season. For each home it measures the kW it contributes in those hours and a peakiness score: whether the home's load above its own baseline across the top-hour window fits inside the battery's power and energy, as opposed to a flat load that stays high for many hours. Each home then climbs a cheapest-first ladder and stops at the first rung that removes its top-hour load. The rungs are, in order: not in top hours (no action); managed charging for the 564 detected Level 2 homes, which shifts the charging block out of the top hours and checks that the daily kWh is still delivered; a summer thermostat event at the assumed 33% shed (summer only, with no winter thermostat rung); a battery, offered only to peaky homes with top-hour load still left; and a flat-high planner watch list that neither software nor a battery covers. The existing 3 kVA rule stays as a gate for homes adding an EV or heat pump. The outputs are a per-home rung CSV, MW of top-N-hour reduction by rung with $/kW from the assumption.* costs, and a stated threshold rule for battery eligibility in place of a long candidate list.

problem: Avangrid builds its grid for a few dozen top system hours, but it cannot tell, home by home, which tool removes that home's load in those hours most cheaply. Today's battery list ranks homes by persistent peak load. Flat, long peaks are the shape a 20 kWh battery handles worst, and on assumed prices that list takes 23 to 33 years to pay back.
specific_user: The Customer Programs and Products Manager. Each season they decide which program to offer each home (summer thermostat DR, EV managed charging, a battery, or a service study) and where the limited program batteries go. solution: Inputs are each home's 8,760-hour AMI load, the temperatures, and the Part 1 class flags (AC, EV L2, electric heat, pool, seasonal). The tool first fixes the target: the top 20 and top 50 system hours in each season, summed over the 25,653 homes and checked against the system peak days Scott named (July 2 and February 7). For each home it walks a fixed ladder in cost order: a summer-only thermostat setback for AC homes, then managed EV charging that moves the Level 2 block out of the top hours, then a battery, then a service study. A home reaches the battery step only when its peak is short and sharp enough for 20.16 kWh at 7.68 kW to cover it, and the battery also has to keep any added EV or heat pump within the 3 kVA rule. Output is a per-home CSV (step, kW removed in the top-N hours, headroom, break-even avoided-upgrade cost), a threshold rule a planner can apply to the full 3 million customers, and a supply curve of MW removed from the top hours at each step.

title: Electric Heat Type Decomposer
problem: Load Research can tell when a home's usage rises with the cold. It cannot tell whether electricity is the home's main heat or a space heater on top of gas or oil, and it cannot tell a heat pump from resistance heat. Those homes set the winter peak, and in this sample the electric-heat count runs anywhere from 2,873 to 4,143 depending on a threshold nobody can defend.
specific_user: Scott, Avangrid's Program Director of Load Research and one of the judges. In office hours he named this split as the problem his team has struggled with. He decides which homes count as primary electric heat in the heating inventory that the Director of Advanced Load Forecasting uses for the winter peak. Customer Programs then uses that inventory to pick resistance-heated homes for heat-pump conversion. Scott doubts winter thermostat events will work, so conversion is the main winter lever left.
solution: Inputs are the existing 25,653 x 8,760 hourly matrix, hourly temperature, the electric-heat flag already in the pipeline, and the heat-pump rebate list. Step 1 pretrains a small 1D-CNN on all 223M readings, using weekly windows of kW plus temperature and a masked-hour reconstruction task. It joins the resulting embeddings to physics features for each home: whether heating kW levels off at the coldest hours (a space heater has a fixed maximum), how much the kW-vs-temperature curve bends as it gets colder (a heat pump loses efficiency and switches on backup strip heat), and lift that follows occupancy rather than temperature. Step 2 trains a two-stage classifier, first primary versus supplemental electric heat and then heat pump versus resistance among primary homes. It is scored on a semi-synthetic benchmark: known heat-type loads, built from the pipeline's own 0.051 kW per F slope plus labeled assumptions, are added to the real winter profiles of homes that do not heat with electricity. The rebate list is used only as a check, never treated as a random sample. Outputs are a per-home heat-type probability file, an inventory with intervals that replaces the single-threshold range, each class's kW in the top 50 winter hours (scored on both the sample's 8 February peak and Scott's 7 February system peak), and a list of resistance-primary homes ranked by the winter-peak kW a heat-pump conversion would remove.

The encoder may separate nothing that the physics features miss. Mitigation: the physics-feature floor ships whatever the encoder does, and the comparison is shown as it came out, win or lose. The deck labels every injected parameter as an assumption and says which results rest on the benchmark and which on real labels. It names gas service flags (already on the readout's data wish list) as the dataset that would validate the split.

The two-stage classifier has to train on the semi-synthetic injections and then run on real homes, so the benchmark score measures how well it separates loads the team wrote itself.
